(1) README "Approach > Temperature design" gives the linear Hk(T) law. It also says a Pc = 1 magnet "calibrates the method to the 150 °C rating, which shifts every onset down by 10.4 °C". So the reference magnet's uncalibrated model temperature of 150 + 10.4 = 160.4 °C is stated there. The workbook does the same (Temperature design!C49/C50, formula for formula), and the README says the port matches the workbook.
(2) The engine's own help text for β (temperature.py line 57, Temperature design!C45) reads "effective, 20–150 °C". So the range is declared, and going past it is how the calibration was designed.
(3) At defaults, only these fall outside the range: the reference magnet (160.43 °C), the aligned case (180.08 °C uncalibrated, 169.65 °C reported) and the single-ring case (153.28 °C uncalibrated, 142.85 °C reported). None of them governs a result:
- The aligned onset (C7/C56) is shown for information only, and it is above the 150 °C rating anyway.
- The single-ring onset only feeds cure_margin = 120.85 °C, checked against ≥ 10.
The governing cases are inside the range: skipping at a model temperature of 112.98 °C (reported onset 102.55 °C, magnet limit 92.55 °C) and pull-out at 123.27 °C.
There is no corrected formula to give, because the literature publishes no coefficient above 150 °C.
verdicts.impact_at_defaults:
No reported value is computed wrong, and every verdict holds under the documented model.
I checked how much this matters by bending the Hcj slope above 150 °C by ±20% (β2 from −0.004 to −0.006 1/°C). Because this changes the Pc = 1 calibration offset, every onset moves:
- Offset: 13.35 / 10.43 / 8.55 °C.
- Skipping onset: 99.63 / 102.55 / 104.42 °C.
- Magnet limit: 89.63 / 92.55 / 94.42 °C.
- Single-ring onset: 140.9 to 144.1 °C. The cure margin stays above 100 °C.
- Aligned onset: 166 to 175 °C.
Governing note, hot-day margin sign, magnet/adhesive life checks and the overall verdict "OK on temperature…" do not change.
One text field could change. In the case where the slope flattens (β2 = −0.004), the magnet limit (89.63 °C) drops just below steady_high_C (89.77 °C). time_to_limit_high would then change from "never: steady state stays below the limit" to a finite time. This is part of the same calibration uncertainty the README already flags ("an analytical estimate, not a guaranteed minimum"), not a defect in the engine.
verdicts.proposed_correction: No change to any formula. Optionally, the README (Approach > Temperature design) could say outright that the Pc = 1 reference point (about 160 °C) and the aligned and single-ring cases extrapolate the linear 20–150 °C Hcj coefficient. It could also say the magnet limit moves about ±3 °C for a ±20% change in the slope above 150 °C, which is enough to flip time_to_limit_high because steady_high sits only 2.8 °C below the limit. The audit check could then be treated as a documented extrapolation instead of a failure.

message: AssertionError: 3 of 12 comparisons failed: library B842SH (N42SH) Br20 vs K&J 1.3-1.33 T [Magnet library / Calculator!C21]: engine=1.29 reference=1.3 rel_err=7.692e-03 tol=0.0e+00 || library BX042SH (N42SH) Br20 vs K&J 1.3-1.33 T [Magnet library / Calculator!C21]: engine=1.29 reference=1.3 rel_err=7.692e-03 tol=0.0e+00 || library BX082SH (N42SH) Br20 vs K&J 1.3-1.33 T [Magnet library / Calculator!C21]: engine=1.29 reference=1.3 rel_err=7.692e-03 tol=0.0e+00

verdicts.reason:
Reproduced from scratch. All three members fail for one reason: the same constant in magcoupling/library.py.

Engine value: MAGNET_LIBRARY rows B842SH, BX042SH and BX082SH (vendor "K&J", grade N42SH) carry br_T = 1.29 T. I confirmed this with lookup("B842SH").br_T, and compute_all(DesignInputs()).model.inner_br_T and outer_br_T are both 1.29. Both default rings are B842SH.

Correct value: I fetched K&J's specification page (kjmagnetics.com/specs.asp) live. It lists N42SH at Br 13.0-13.3 kG (1.30-1.33 T), N42 at 13.0-13.2 kG and N52 at 14.5-14.8 kG. The B842SH product page gives "Br Max 13,200 Gauss", grade N42SH, 150 °C. So 1.29 T is below the vendor's own published minimum for its own part: |1.29-1.30|/1.30 = 7.69e-3, which matches the check message exactly.

The check is not at fault. Its reference table KJ_BR_RANGE_T in audit/references/demag_adhesive.py matches the live K&J data, and a clamp-to-range test with tol=0 is reasonable here. The other N42 and N52 rows (1.30, 1.45) sit at the bottom of their ranges and pass.

This is not a harmless conservative choice. A lower Br lowers the pull-out torque, which is conservative for the hot-minimum check. It also lowers the cold-high torque that sizes the shaft clamp and the adhesive bond, which is non-conservative. The row is also not labelled as assumed or a placeholder, unlike Calibration test_temp_C. The same 1.29 appears in Calibration!C21 (the prototype B842SH) and in the manual Br fallbacks at Calculator!C17 and C27. Those look like a copied value, not a sourced one.

Severity is low. The torque change (+1.56 % at 1.30 T, +3.9 % at the 1.315 T mid-range) is well inside the 15 % symmetric variation allowance.
verdicts.impact_at_defaults:
I checked this by editing MAGNET_LIBRARY in memory only (scratch script br_patch.py) and running compute_all(DesignInputs()), which uses backiron=1, B842SH/B842SH, 50 °C and 10 poles.

With Br = 1.30 T:
- Pull-out torque: 2.6473 -> 2.6885 N·m (+1.556 %).
- Torque at 20 °C: 2.8487 -> 2.8930 N·m.
- Hot-low torque: 2.2502 -> 2.2852 N·m. hot_min_check stays 'Below hot minimum' (required minimum 2.5 N·m).
- Cold-high torque: 3.7647 -> 3.8233 N·m.
- Governing temperature limit: 92.55 -> 93.06 °C. This mostly comes from the h_ref/offset calibration. 'Magnets govern (skipping case).' is unchanged, and the temperature verdict 'OK on temperature...' is unchanged.
- Adhesive fatigue_screen: 'OK: 8x margin' -> 'OK: 7x margin'.
- gap_sweep row 3 (1.25 mm corner gap): 2.4619 -> 2.5002 N·m, and its status changes from 'below hot minimum' to 'nominal: test needed'.
- The clamp recommendation is unchanged at 1.30 T.

A scan in 0.0005 T steps shows clamps.recommended flips at Br ≈ 1.302 T (cold-high 3.835 N·m), from 'ISO 4762 M4 x 12, class 12.9' to 'None: enlarge the boss or the clamp length'. head_check and vent_port go blank at the same point. So with the mid-range 1.315 T or the product-page 1.32 T (torque +3.9 % / +4.7 %), the default design loses its clamp-screw recommendation. 'Below hot minimum' does not change at any Br from 1.29 to 1.33 T.
verdicts.proposed_correction: Minimal fix: in magcoupling/library.py, set br_T to at least K&J's published N42SH minimum of 1.30 T for B842SH, BX042SH and BX082SH. Use 1.30 as a guaranteed minimum, or about 1.315 T if the library is meant to hold nominal values. For consistency, give Calibration.br_T (Calibration!C21, the prototype B842SH) the same value. That changes nothing at defaults, because backiron=1 uses f_cal_original. Also give the manual_inner_br_T and manual_outer_br_T defaults (C17, C27) the same value. Those are fallbacks only and have no effect at defaults. Torque scales as (Br_new/1.29)^2: 1.01556 at 1.30 T and 1.03914 at 1.315 T. Ideally rerun fields3d.run and apply_to_inputs so the h_rev inputs match the new Br. Otherwise the demag calibration offset moves the temperature limits a little on its own.

verdicts.reason:
The group has one member. It is an input-data discrepancy, not a formula bug, and I tried and failed to break the check:
(1) The reference data is right. I fetched kjmagnetics.com/specs.asp live. It lists N42SH at Br 13.0-13.3 kGs, N42 at 13.0-13.2 and N52 at 14.5-14.8. This matches KJ_BR_RANGE_T in audit/references/demag_adhesive.py:81 exactly, and 13.0 kG = 1.30 T, so the units are right.
(2) The engine field is right. MagnetSpec.br_T in magcoupling/library.py:28,38,39 is what model.py:186 resolves into Calculator!C21/C31.
(3) The tolerance is right. It is a range-containment test (clamp to [lo, hi], then tol 0), so any value inside the range passes. There is no numerics or geometry involved.
I reproduced the failure with pytest: B842SH, BX042SH and BX082SH carry 1.29 T, below K&J's N42SH minimum of 1.30 T.
The only weakness in K&J's data is that the B842SH product page says "Br max 13,200 G" while the spec page gives 13.3 kG max. That affects the upper bound only, not the 1.30 T floor that is violated.
The library's own convention also points to an error. Its other K&J rows use the grade minimum (N42 = 1.30, N52 = 1.45), so the N42SH rows at 1.29 are the odd ones out.
The value is not simply conservative. metal_design.py:190-191 applies a symmetric ±15 % variation around the nominal torque. A Br below the range lowers the hot-low torque, which is conservative, but it also lowers the cold-high torque, which is not: that value feeds the clamp and bond-shear checks.
Side effect to report: running pytest rewrote audit/out/results.json through a conftest hook (audit/tests/conftest.py:46). Other skeptics running in parallel are overwriting the same file. candidate_groups.json was not touched.
verdicts.impact_at_defaults:
Defaults use backiron=1, so f_cal = 0.95 and the Calibration sheet does not cancel the change. Both rings are B842SH, and torque scales with Br².

Br 1.29 to 1.30 T (K&J minimum):
- Pull-out at operating temperature: 2.6473 to 2.6885 N·m (+1.56 %)
- Pull-out at 20 °C: 2.8487 to 2.8930 N·m
- Hot-low with variation: 2.2502 to 2.2852 N·m. It stays "Below hot minimum".
- Cold-high with variation: 3.7647 to 3.8233 N·m
- Gearbox ripple: 0.5573 to 0.5660 N·m
- Governing temperature limit: 92.55 to 93.06 °C, and hot-day margin 27.55 to 28.06 °C
- No verdict text changes. The clamp screw stays "ISO 4762 M4 x 12, class 12.9", and the clearance, cup-wall and temperature verdicts are unchanged.

The margin is very small: the clamp verdict flips at Br of about 1.3025 T. At the K&J mid-range 1.315 T (Arnold's N42SH nominal is 1.31 T):
- Pull-out: 2.7509 N·m (+3.9 %)
- Cold-high: 3.912 N·m, and clamp_screw changes to "None: enlarge the boss or the clamp length"
- Hot_min_check is still "Below hot minimum".

So the 1.29 T value hides a clamp-sizing failure across almost the whole published Br range.
verdicts.proposed_correction:
Set br_T for the N42SH library rows (B842SH, BX042SH, BX082SH in magcoupling/library.py) to at least K&J's minimum of 1.30 T. This matches how the N42 and N52 rows are filled.

Because metal_design applies a symmetric ±15 % variation around the nominal torque, a central value of about 1.315 T is more defensible. Alternatively, run the cold-high, clamp and adhesive checks at the top of the range (1.33 T) and the hot-low check at the bottom (1.30 T).

Change the manual defaults (Calculator!C17/C27, model.py:42,46) and the prototype Br (Calibration!C21, calibration.py:33) to the same value, so the no-iron calibration path stays consistent. There, Br cancels between the calibration factor and the design only if both are changed together.

verdicts.reason: All three failing members come from one data value. The N42SH rows B842SH, BX042SH and BX082SH in magcoupling/library.py store br_T = 1.29 T. K&J publishes 1.30 to 1.33 T for that grade, so the stored value sits 0.01 T (0.77%) below K&J's minimum. The check itself is correct: 1.29 really is outside the K&J range. But nothing is wrong with any formula. The engine copies the workbook's Magnet library data exactly. The snapshot tests/reference_values.json has Calculator!C21 = C31 = C17 = C27 = 1.29 and Calibration!C21 = 1.29, and the README's stated aim is "Same numbers as the workbook". The value is a supplier-data input rounded down to the conservative side. It lies inside the 1.28/1.29 to 1.32 T range that common industry N42SH grade tables and datasheets give (I did not check those tables in this session). The library.py docstring treats rows as user-editable ("Add rows freely"). One caveat: the README's "Inputs that are placeholders" table does not list library Br explicitly, so the declaration is implicit. The README should add it. Only B842SH affects the default design. BX042SH and BX082SH are unused at defaults.
verdicts.impact_at_defaults: I recomputed with B842SH Br patched in memory; no files were changed. At Br 1.30 T (K&J minimum): pull-out at 50 C goes from 2.6473 to 2.6885 N·m (+1.56%, torque scales with Br^2). Pull-out at 20 C goes from 2.849 to 2.893. Hot low with variation goes from 2.2502 to 2.2852 N·m and is still 'Below hot minimum'. Cold high goes from 3.7647 to 3.8233 N·m. The governing temperature limit goes from 92.55 to 93.06 C, with the temperature verdict unchanged. The clamp stays 'ISO 4762 M4 x 12, class 12.9'. No verdict text changes. At Br 1.31 T (Arnold/K&J nominal): hot low is 2.3205 (still below the minimum) and cold high is 3.882 N·m. The clamp recommendation then changes to 'None: enlarge the boss or the clamp length'. So 1.29 T is conservative for torque but slightly non-conservative for clamp and bond sizing, which run off the cold high torque.
verdicts.proposed_correction: No engine formula change. Pick one of two fixes. (a) Keep 1.29 T as a deliberate conservative value, and add library Br (and calibration.br_T) to the README's "Inputs that are placeholders" table. Say there that K&J's N42SH range is 1.30-1.33 T and that cold high torque, and so clamp and bond sizing, should be checked at nominal or maximum Br. (b) Change the N42SH rows to 1.30 T (K&J minimum) in both the workbook's Magnet library sheet and library.py, then regenerate the parity snapshot. Changing library.py alone would break parity on Calculator!C21/C31 and every downstream cell.

message: AssertionError: 1 of 1 comparisons failed: fatigue screen with endurance 0.1 (reference margin 3.7707): engine 'OK: 8x margin', expected 'CHECK' (1 = holds) [Temperature design!C91, Temperature design!C195]: engine=0.0 reference=1.0 rel_err=1.000e+00 tol=0.0e+00

verdicts.reason:
Reproduced. The group has one member and a single cause. In magcoupling/temperature.py line 443 the C91 fatigue screen hard-codes the endurance fraction: `fat = 0.2 * sel.lap_shear_MPa / tau_b`. It ignores the input `temperature.adhesive_life.fatigue_endurance` (Temperature design!C195, default 0.2, "Fatigue endurance at 10^8+ cycles, share of static strength"). That same quantity is read from the input in C196 (hot margin = lap x hot_retained x endurance / amp) and C202 (daily screen, lap x endurance). The C91 life (C90 shear reversals, about 3.3e8 cycles) falls in C195's 10^8+ cycle range, so C91 needs the same fraction. The hard-coded 0.2 is just a copy of the input's default.

What I ran (python -c against compute_all, no audit helpers): I recomputed tau_b from the engine's own C81/C83/C84 outputs. Ft = 3.764716 / (8 x 0.011735) = 32.0811 N, and tau = 32.0811 / 80.645 = 0.397806 MPa, which matches the engine's C86 exactly. Static ratio = 15 / 0.397806 = 37.7068.
- At defaults (endurance 0.2): engine margin = 0.2 x 37.7068 = 7.5414, giving "OK: 8x margin". The reference gives the same.
- At endurance 0.1: the engine still says "OK: 8x margin", because its margin stays at 7.5414. The reference margin is 0.1 x 37.7068 = 3.7707, which is below 4, so the result should be "CHECK". C196 does react to the change (2.426, "CHECK: get hot fatigue data"), which shows the inconsistency within the engine itself.
- At endurance 0.15 the engine says 8x and the reference 6x. At 0.25 the engine says 8x and the reference 9x.

I also ran the audit test with pytest and it fails with exactly this message. The audit's own derivation checks out: margin = C195 x C78 / C86, with Excel TEXT(x,"0") rounding.

Caveat: I don't have the original .xlsx. The port may be copying a literal 0.2 from the workbook's C91 formula. Even if so, it is still a formula defect (an input the user can edit that one screen silently ignores), not a question of model approximation. It is low severity. Nothing else in the engine reads fatigue_screen; it is a display string only.
verdicts.impact_at_defaults: None. The C195 default is 0.2, so the corrected margin is 0.2 x 15 / 0.397806 = 7.5414 at defaults, the same as the engine's, and C91 still reads "OK: 8x margin". No verdict text changes at defaults: no 'Below hot minimum', governing-limit or summary text depends on C91. Divergence starts only when the user edits C195. The text differs from "8x" for any endurance outside [0.1989, 0.2254), and the verdict flips from OK to "CHECK" for endurance below 4/37.7068 = 0.10608 (for example 0.1 gives margin 3.7707, "CHECK").
verdicts.proposed_correction: In compute (temperature.py line 443) replace `fat = 0.2 * sel.lap_shear_MPa / tau_b` with `fat = ti.adhesive_life.fatigue_endurance * sel.lap_shear_MPa / tau_b`. That is C91 = C195 x C78 / C86 (equivalently C195 x C89), with the screen unchanged: "OK: TEXT(fat,"0")x margin" if fat >= 4, else "CHECK". Use ti.adhesive_life here because the local `al` is only assigned later, in the adhesive-life block. For the Rust port, fix it the same way. If strict parity with the workbook is required, record it as a known workbook defect (a hard-coded literal duplicating an input) and add a regression test that varies C195, for example to 0.1, expecting "CHECK".

verdicts.reason:
I tried to find a fault in the check and could not; the engine is at fault. The group has one member, so there is only one cause to judge.

What the engine does: temperature.py:443 computes the C91 screen margin as `fat = 0.2 * sel.lap_shear_MPa / tau_b`. The 0.2 is typed in as a literal. The same quantity already exists as an input: C195, `adhesive_life.fatigue_endurance`, labelled "Fatigue endurance at 10^8+ cycles, share of static strength", with a default of 0.2. The hot fatigue margin C196 (line 526) and the daily-cycle screen C202 (line 530) both read C195. C91 is the room-temperature screen over the life shear reversals in C90 (about 3.3e8 cycles, so it is in the 10^8+ regime too). It should use the same share. No separate room-temperature endurance input exists that would explain the literal.

Why the check holds up:
- **Same load.** The reference bond shear from `_bond_shear_reference` is 0.39780636770337496 MPa, bit-identical to the engine's `bond_shear_MPa` (C86). Lap shear is 15 MPa in both.
- **Right fields.** The check reads the correct engine field (`adhesive.fatigue_screen`, cell C91) and the correct input path.
- **Same rounding.** The reference's text rounding (Excel TEXT "0", round half away from zero) matches the engine's `_text0` at these margins.
- **No tolerance or numerics issue.** It is an exact text comparison, and nothing iterates.
- **Plausible input.** An endurance of 0.1 is a reasonable value, and the engine's own C196 responds to it: it drops to 2.43 and reads "CHECK: get hot fatigue data".

The only difference between engine and reference is the literal 0.2. Varying the endurance shows C91 never moves:

| Endurance | Engine C91 | Correct margin | Correct C91 |
|---|---|---|---|
| 0.1 | "OK: 8x margin" | 3.77 | "CHECK" |
| 0.15 | "OK: 8x margin" | 5.66 | "OK: 6x margin" |
| 0.3 | "OK: 8x margin" | 11.31 | "OK: 11x margin" |

This is not a modelling approximation: the literal simply duplicates an input. It has no effect at defaults, and gives a wrong verdict whenever a user changes C195.
verdicts.impact_at_defaults: None. C195 defaults to 0.2, so the C91 margin stays at 7.5414 and the text stays "OK: 8x margin". No verdict text changes at defaults, and neither do C89, C196, C197 or C202. The fix only matters once a user edits C195. For example, at 0.1 C91 flips from "OK: 8x margin" to "CHECK".
verdicts.proposed_correction: In the workbook, C91 should reference C195 (fatigue_endurance × lap shear / bond shear, i.e. fatigue_endurance × C78/C86 or the equivalent cells) instead of the literal 0.2. In the engine, temperature.py:443 becomes `fat = ti.adhesive_life.fatigue_endurance * sel.lap_shear_MPa / tau_b`. It has to read `ti.adhesive_life`, because the local `al` is only assigned later, at line 523.

verdicts.reason:
This group has one member and one cause, and I reproduced it. In magcoupling/temperature.py line 443 the 22 °C fatigue screen (Temperature design!C91) is computed as `fat = 0.2 * sel.lap_shear_MPa / tau_b`, with 0.2 typed in directly. The editable input `temperature.adhesive_life.fatigue_endurance` (C195, default 0.2, labelled "Fatigue endurance at 10^8+ cycles, share of static strength") is ignored there. The hot fatigue margin (C196), its screen (C197) and the daily screen all do read that input. Engine output: at endurance 0.2, 0.1, 0.106 and 0.3, C91 always says 'OK: 8x margin'. The same input moves C196 from 4.85 to 2.43, and C197 changes to 'CHECK: get hot fatigue data'. A margin built from the input would be 0.1 × 37.7068 = 3.7707, which is below 4 and gives 'CHECK'.

I looked for a benign explanation and found none in the README. "Approach" does not mention a fixed 20 % endurance for C91. The placeholders table does not list fatigue_endurance; it lists only hot_strength_retained. "Differences from the workbook" says everything else is formula-for-formula. The engine probably copies the workbook's own formula: the workbook note F91 says "Assumes a shear endurance of about 20 % of static strength at 10^8 cycles", and the parity snapshot holds values only, so parity at defaults cannot tell the two formulas apart. That note is not carried into the engine help text (C91 has none, and C195's help is empty) or into the README.

C195 describes the same quantity as the F91 assumption, and the workbook's C197 note says "Same 4x criterion as the 22 °C screen". So the engine keeps two copies of one value, and a GUI user who edits fatigue_endurance gets a stale C91 verdict with no warning. This is a real but latent consistency defect, most likely inherited from the workbook, not a declared approximation or placeholder. The check itself is sound: the reference margin and the 'OK'/'CHECK' threshold of 4 match the engine's own formatting.
verdicts.impact_at_defaults: None. At the default C195 = 0.2 the corrected margin is 0.2 × 37.7068 = 7.5414, so C91 still reads 'OK: 8x margin'. The 1e-9 parity snapshot and every verdict text stay the same, including 'Below hot minimum', C197 'OK' and the summary. The fix only shows when the input is edited: C91 turns 'CHECK' once fatigue_endurance < 4 / 37.7068 ≈ 0.1061. For example, 0.1 gives margin 3.77 and 'CHECK', where today it gives 'OK: 8x margin'.
verdicts.proposed_correction: In compute (temperature.py ~line 443), replace the literal with the input: `fat = ti.adhesive_life.fatigue_endurance * sel.lap_shear_MPa / tau_b`, which is C91 = C195 × C78 / C86 against the same ≥ 4 'OK: Nx margin' / 'CHECK' test. If workbook-literal parity is to be kept, then instead at minimum: (a) add help text to C91 saying it assumes a fixed 20 % endurance independent of C195, (b) add help text to fatigue_endurance saying it drives only C196, C197 and the daily screen, and (c) list the difference in the README either way. With the fix, add an entry to "Differences from the workbook", because the workbook hard-codes 20 % per its F91 note.

message:
AssertionError: adhesive shear modulus vs Loctite AA 326 + SF 7649 TDS (Henkel TDS LOCTITE AA 326 (Aug-2020): heat-ageing data at 100 and 120 degC (no higher), Tg not published, tensile modulus ISO 527-2 = 300 N/mm^2, elongation 135 %, lap shear 15.2 N/mm^2 with Activator 7649 on one side, recommended bondline 0.1 mm.) [Temperature design!C96]: engine=0.55 reference=0.10769230769230768 rel_err=4.107e+00 tol=7.1e-02
assert 0.55 <= 0.11538461538461538

verdicts.reason:
Reproduced. The group has one member, and the problem is in the engine's default data, not its code. The engine default is MismatchInputs.adhesive_shear_modulus_GPa = 0.55 GPa (magcoupling/temperature.py:102, Temperature design!C96, blank help text). It is not listed in the README's placeholder table.

I checked the correct value against the source myself. I downloaded Henkel's LOCTITE AA 326 TDS (Aug-2020, datasheets.tdx.henkel.com/LOCTITE-AA-326-en_GL.pdf) and read it. It gives tensile modulus ISO 527-2 = 300 N/mm^2, elongation 135 %, lap shear 15.2 N/mm^2 with 7649 on one side, and a recommended gap of 0.1 mm, so the audit's reference data is correct. The TDS gives no shear modulus. Using G = E/(2(1+nu)) with E = 0.300 GPa: nu 0.3 gives 0.1154, nu 0.4 gives 0.1071, nu 0.5 gives 0.1000 GPa. The engine's 0.55 is 4.8 to 5.5 times stiffer than any of these. For comparison, the EA 9514 alternative (E = 1.46 GPa, nu about 0.327) gives 0.549 GPa. So C96 looks like it was taken from the heat-cure epoxy or a generic epoxy value, not from the default AA 326.

The formula is not at fault. I wrote my own Volkersen closed form with python -c, using lam = sqrt(G/eta*(1/(E1 t1)+1/(E2 t2))) and tau = G*da*dT*tanh(lam L/2)/(lam eta). At G = 0.55 it matches the engine to about 1e-15: C104 = 46.1265 MPa and C105 = 26.7283 MPa, at worst swing 70.55 C and bondlines 0.05 and 0.1 mm.

The check itself is sound. ISO 527-2 modulus is a small-strain value, which suits a linear-elastic shear-lag model, and the check accepts any nu from 0.3 to 0.5. The one structural catch is that C96 is a single input shared by all candidates. So 0.55 is roughly right only when EA 9514 is selected. Selecting EA 9514 gives C104 = 104.6 MPa against its 45 MPa lap shear, which still reads 'Above'.
verdicts.impact_at_defaults:
At defaults (AA 326, current bondline 0.05 mm, recommended bondline 0.1 mm, worst swing 70.55 C, lap shear 15 MPa):
- C104 peak end shear at the current bondline falls from 46.13 to 11.67 MPa (10.89 to 12.44 over the nu band).
- C105 peak end shear at the recommended bondline falls from 26.73 to 6.07 MPa (5.65 to 6.48).
- The C106 verdict text changes from 'Above the lap-shear strength at the block ends' to 'Below the lap-shear strength'. The flip happens when G drops below 0.142 GPa, and every G in the AA 326 band (at most 0.115) is below that.

The group has one member and I reproduced it: engine/exact is 0.955909, a 4.41% shortfall against the 2% TOL_MODEL.

1. Engine value, re-derived by hand. I wrote the planar formula from the README in a scratch script, using the Calibration defaults (20 x B842SH, apothem 9.85 mm, t 3.17 mm, w 6.35 mm, L 12.7 mm, Br 1.29 T, flat gap 1.4 mm). The derived values are:
   - r_face 13.02 mm, a_o 14.42 mm, R_gap 13.72 mm
   - fill_i 0.8838, fill_o 0.6314
   - k1 = 5/R_gap
   - S = (1-e^-kt)^2 e^-kg / 2
   This gives C43 = 1.880350 N·m, the same as calibration.compute (1.880350196). The last digits differ only because the value of mu0 differs.

2. Correct value, from an independent solver. I built a 2D Coulombian model: magnetic surface charges on the front and back faces of every flat block, composite Gauss-Legendre quadrature, and the torque on the inner ring taken as the sum of r x mu0*sigma*H_outer. It uses no engine or audit code, and it is a different method from the audit's Maxwell stress on current sheets. Results:
   - 154.88823 N·m/m at 90 electrical degrees, unchanged from nsub 8 to 32. An angle scan confirms the peak is at 90 degrees.
   - Times L, that is 1.967081 N·m, the same as the audit reference to about 1e-15.
   So the 4.4% gap is real.

3. The cause is the planar approximation, not a bug. I kept t, w, g and the pole pitch fixed and increased the pole count and radius. The planar formula (n up to 13) divided by the exact 2D torque moves towards 1 as the radius grows, roughly 4x less error per doubling of the pole count:

| Poles N | planar / exact |
|---|---|
| 10 | 0.9564 |
| 20 | 0.9895 |
| 40 | 0.9974 |
| 80 | 0.99936 |
| 160 | 0.99984 |
| 320 | 0.99997 |

   So the engine's algebra (square-wave B_n, the free-space S_n, the 2*pi*R^2*L lever arm, and the fill definitions) is exact in the planar limit. The 4.4% is the curvature error of unrolling a 10-pole ring with t/R_gap = 0.23. Stopping at harmonic 5 instead of 13 accounts for only 0.05% (0.9559 vs 0.9564).

The engine implements the documented model: README Torque model steps 1-3, which the README calls "an analytical estimate". So this is a known limitation of the model, not an engine error.

verdicts.reason:
I reproduced the failures and all eight members have the same cause. The engine unrolls the ring into a flat slab (k = n·(N/2)/R_g, area 2π·R_g²), and curvature adds a planar-vs-cylindrical error. The engine code has no bug. model.py:200-224 matches the documented formulas in README.md steps 2-3, and the module docstring says it is "the workbook's 2D slab model".

What I ran (scratch script in my temp dir; the engine was only called, never edited):
(1) Pulled the engine's radii and S_n for each (circuit, gap) case, with N=10 so m = 5, 15, 25. I recomputed the planar S from scratch. It matches the engine exactly.
(2) Derived the free-space cylindrical factor by hand from ring charges: volume charge -M/r plus surface charges ±M, with the order-m log-kernel potential, interaction energy and T = m·W0. The result is S = m²/(2(m²-1))·(x1b^(m+1) - x1a^(m+1))·(x2a^(1-m) - x2b^(1-m)), identical to the audit's reference formula.

- Free space, 3.0 mm, S1: 0.0763386 vs 0.0763319 (engine 0.078396)
- Steel, 0.5 mm, S1: 0.334806 vs 0.334806 (engine 0.341533)
- Steel, 1.4 mm, S1: 0.237717 vs 0.237718 (engine 0.244488)
- Steel, 3.0 mm, S1: 0.135060 vs 0.135059 (engine 0.141696)

The planar/cylindrical excess is always positive, so the planar model overstates torque:
- Free space: +0.84 / +0.52 / +0.08 % at 0.5 mm, +1.35 / +1.14 / +0.62 % at 1.4 mm, +2.70 / +3.44 / +3.22 % at 3.0 mm (n = 1 / 3 / 5).

verdicts.proposed_correction:
This is optional, since the model is working as designed. To remove the curvature bias, replace the planar geometry_factor with the exact closed-form cylindrical factor for radial arcs. Use m = n·N/2 and x = r/R_g, with r1a = C54 - C20, r1b = C54, r2a = C56, r2b = C60.

Free space:
S = m²/(2(m²-1))·(x1b^(m+1) - x1a^(m+1))·(x2a^(1-m) - x2b^(1-m))

Steel at the magnet backs, with ρ1 = x1a and ρ2 = x2b:
- u1(s) = (s/ρ1)^m - (ρ1/s)^m
- u2(s) = (ρ2/s)^m - (s/ρ2)^m

(1) Geometry matches. At every case the arcs have t_i = t_o = C20 = 3.17 mm. The gap C56-C54 equals the engine's face_gap_mm exactly (0.5/1.4/3.0). C64 sits exactly mid-gap (13.57/14.02/14.82 mm). The steel circles sit at the magnet backs (C54-C20 = 10.15 mm and C60), which is the same idealisation as the engine's sinh(k(t_i+t_o+g)).
(2) Order and cells are right. The code uses m = n*N//2 = 5n, which is the same as the engine's k = n(N/2)/R_gap, so k*R_gap = m. Cells map correctly: C74/C80/C86 = s{n}_iron and C75/C81/C87 = s{n}_free.
(3) Normalisation is the same on both sides: torque/L = B_i B_o/(2 mu0) S 2 pi R_gap^2, as in the engine's C90.
(4) The reference is exact. I derived the free-space closed form by hand: charge potential (s r'/2m)(r</r>)^m, then interaction energy mu0∫rho2 phi1. I got S = m^2/(2(m^2-1))(x1b^(m+1)-x1a^(m+1))(x2a^(1-m)-x2b^(1-m)), identical to cylindrical_s_factor. The steel form is backed by the audit's sliced-ring Maxwell-stress sanity test, which converges at second order in slice count.
(5) The residual is real second-order curvature, not a numerical artefact. I held k, t and g fixed and scaled R_gap by 1, 2, 4 and 8. err*R^2 stays constant: free space 0.01342, 0.01319, 0.01313, 0.01312; steel 0.02848, 0.02794, 0.02781, 0.02778. With R_gap only 14 mm against dr of about 4.3 mm, that gives the observed +2.0% to +4.9%. I recomputed all 18 parametrisations and they match the reported numbers.
(6) test_planar_s_factor_is_exact_planar_limit passes, so the engine formula is correct in its own planar limit.

Caveat on what the check means: the reference is radially magnetised arcs, not the engine's flat parallel blocks. The deciding exact flat-block checks (groups 22/23) show the engine UNDER-predicting by 2.3% (steel at the backs) to 3.9% (free space). That is the opposite sign to this +2.8% S_1 excess. So the curvature term is partly cancelled by flat-block and corner effects, and this check is best read as a diagnostic breakdown, not a separate error to fix.
verdicts.impact_at_defaults: At defaults (steel, 1.4 mm), S_1 is 2.85% above exact. Replacing all three S_n with the exact cylindrical factors lowers shear by 2.76% (198294 to 192831 Pa) and pull-out at operating temperature from 2.647 to 2.574 N·m. In free space the drop is 1.33% (1.697 to 1.675 N·m), and the prototype-fitted C42 would largely absorb it. That swap would move the engine further from the exact flat-block 2D section, which it already under-predicts by 2.3% to 3.9%. So the change is not recommended, and I did not recompute whether any verdict text would change.
verdicts.proposed_correction: No engine change. Report this as a documented curvature approximation of the planar S_n, about O(((t+g/2)/R_gap)^2) and roughly 2-5% at R_gap of about 14 mm with 10 poles. Optionally add a line to the README naming the approximation, or reclassify this check as a diagnostic that sits under the flat-block pull-out checks rather than a standalone TOL_MODEL pass/fail.

verdicts.reason: All 8 members have the same cause: finite-radius curvature. The engine uses the unrolled planar S_n, and the audit compares it with the exact cylindrical S_n for the same arcs. It also calls the result "an analytical estimate, not a guaranteed minimum". I checked that the engine implements exactly that model. verdicts.impact_at_defaults: Default design is steel, 1.4 mm gap, R_g 14.02 mm, 10 poles. The planar S_n read high by 2.85% (n=1), 0.62% (n=3) and 0.37% (n=5). verdicts.reason:
I reproduced the failures and all eight members have the same cause. The engine unrolls the ring into a flat slab (k = n·(N/2)/R_g, area 2π·R_g²), and curvature adds a planar-vs-cylindrical error. What I ran (scratch script in my temp dir; the engine was only called, never edited):
(1) Pulled the engine's radii and S_n for each (circuit, gap) case, with N=10 so m = 5, 15, 25. I recomputed the planar S from scratch. It matches the engine exactly.

- Steel, 0.5 mm, S1: 0.334806 vs 0.334806 (engine 0.341533)
- Steel, 1.4 mm, S1: 0.237717 vs 0.237718 (engine 0.244488)
- Steel, 3.0 mm, S1: 0.135060 vs 0.135059 (engine 0.141696)

- Free space: +0.84 / +0.52 / +0.08 % at 0.5 mm, +1.35 / +1.14 / +0.62 % at 1.4 mm, +2.70 / +3.44 / +3.22 % at 3.0 mm (n = 1 / 3 / 5).
- Steel: +2.01 / +0.14 / -0.07 % at 0.5 mm, +2.85 / +0.63 / +0.37 % at 1.4 mm, +4.91 / +2.66 / +2.75 % at 3.0 mm.

verdicts.proposed_correction:
This is optional, since the model is working as designed. To remove the curvature bias, replace the planar geometry_factor with the exact closed-form cylindrical factor for radial arcs. Use m = n·N/2 and x = r/R_g, with r1a = C54 - C20, r1b = C54, r2a = C56, r2b = C60.

Free space:
S = m²/(2(m²-1))·(x1b^(m+1) - x1a^(m+1))·(x2a^(1-m) - x2b^(1-m))

Steel at the magnet backs, with ρ1 = x1a and ρ2 = x2b:
- u1(s) = (s/ρ1)^m - (ρ1/s)^m
- u2(s) = (ρ2/s)^m - (s/ρ2)^m
- p = [s·u(s)] across the ring minus ∫u ds across the ring
- Q = (ρ2/ρ1)^m
- S = p_i·p_o / (2(Q - 1/Q))

The cost is the same kind of closed form the engine already uses, and it reduces to the current formulas in the planar limit. Otherwise, keep the planar model and add one line to the README saying it ignores curvature and overstates S by about 1-5 % at N=10, R_g ≈ 14 mm.

verdicts.reason:
I reproduced all five members from scratch, and every member has the same cause: the engine's planar (flat-slab) harmonic model is being compared with real faceted cylindrical rings. The engine does not implement that model wrongly.

What I ran (scratch scripts in the session scratchpad: t3rc1.py, sweep.py, rest.py, cyl.py; no repo files touched):

(1) Engine side, derived independently. I worked out the free-space two-slab shear from the interaction energy. The field above slab 1 is B_y = (Br1n/2)(1-e^{-k t1}) e^{-k y} cos kx. Then W/area = -<M2.B1> integrated over slab 2, and tau_n = -dW/dd gives Br_in·Br_on/(4 mu0)·(1-e^{-k t_i})(1-e^{-k t_o})·e^{-k g}·sin(n k1 d). This is exactly the engine's S_free (with its /2) times Bi·Bo/(2 mu0). My own implementation, using R_g = r_face + g/2, fill at the mid-magnet radius and the 1-c_end·pitch/L end factor, reproduces the engine to every printed digit: T2D = 1.912786 and raw pull-out = 1.713773 N·m at defaults (free space, 20 C, 1.4 mm face gap).

(2) Correct value, computed a different way from the audit. I built magpylib Cuboid rings and took the torque as -dW/dtheta, where W = -∫ M·B_inner dV. That is my own composite Gauss-Legendre volume quadrature with a central difference. The audit instead integrates surface charges. I cross-checked against magpylib.getFT (1.777465 vs 1.777459) and refined the quadrature until values were stable to about 1e-7.

Results: every member reproduced exactly.
- Gap sweep, engine/3D - 1: -6.886%, -5.536%, -3.583%, -0.103%, +3.331%, +7.009%.
- Pole sweep for 6-16 poles: +3.044%, -4.088%, -3.583%, -2.342%, -1.238%, -0.393%.
- 2D limit (3D slope over L = 30-60 mm, times L): 1.991253 vs engine 1.912786, -3.941%.
- Prototype (hub 9.85 mm, 3D peak at exactly 18 deg): 1.755382 vs 1.688898, -3.787%.
- Decay ratios T(g)/T(1.4 mm) at 6, 10, 30 and 100 mm: +17.9%, +40.2%, +299%, +7101%.

(3) Where the error comes from. I also wrote the exact 2D cylindrical solution for radially magnetized arc rings with the same Br, fill and radii: T/L = pi·Bi·Bo·m²/(2 mu0 (m²-1))·(R2^{m+1}-R1^{m+1})(R3^{1-m}-R4^{1-m}). At 1.4 mm it gives 1.8874. The exact flat-block 2D value is 1.9913, and the planar model's 1.9128 sits between the two.
- At small gaps, faceting dominates. The inner block corners sit 0.37 mm closer than the face gap, so the engine reads low.
- At larger gaps, curvature dominates. Planar e^{-kg} decays more slowly than (R2/R3)^{m-1}, so the engine reads high. The sign flips near 2.4 mm.
- Harmonic truncation is negligible: 25 harmonics vs 3 changes the result by <0.1%.

The decay failure is out of the model's domain. At face gaps of 30-100 mm the outer ring would be 60-240 mm across, far outside the 43 mm envelope. There R_g grows with g, so k·g levels off near N and the planar torque tends to a small nonzero constant. The absolute engine value at 100 mm is 2.2e-4 N·m. Switching to the 'correct' cylindrical formula would not fix the design-gap error: it would be about -5.2% against the exact flat-block 2D value, worse than the engine's -3.9%. So no formula swap is clearly more accurate, and I found no engine_error.

The block-centre radius a_i + t/2 is the same radius the engine uses for its fill factor. The comparison angle π/N is the engine's sin(nπ/2) pull-out point. The prototype check uses gap_definition=1 in both the engine and the audit.

(3) The engine's free-space S_n = (1-e^-kt_i)(1-e^-kt_o)e^-kg/2 with J_i·J_o/(2 mu0) matches my own derivation of two normally magnetized slabs under the surface-charge model. So this is not an engine error.

The members do not share one cause, though. I split each error into a 2D part and an end-factor part, using the 3D slope and T3D/(slope·L).
- Members 4 (-3.94%) and 5 (-3.79%, prototype) are purely the 2D harmonic amplitude. It is nearly constant at -3.8% to -4.2% for face gaps of 0.6-4.4 mm. This is the same cause as group 22 (test_pullout_2d_matches_flat_block_reference).
- Member 1 (gap sweep) gets its trend and its worst row from the end factor 1 - c_end·τp/L. That factor barely changes with gap, while the 3D end deficit grows with gap. At 4.4 mm the engine's f_end is 0.8848 against 0.7955 in 3D (+11.2%), on top of a 2D error of -3.8%, giving +7.0% overall. At 0.6 mm it is -3.2% on top of -3.8%, giving -6.9%.
- Member 3 (pole sweep): the worst row, 8 poles at -4.1%, is mostly end factor (f_end -3.4%, 2D -0.7%). At 6 poles a 2D error of +16.8% and an f_end error of -11.8% largely cancel.
- Member 2 (decay): the 6 mm and 10 mm rows come mostly from the end factor (+16.6% and +30.0%). The 30 mm and 100 mm rows come from the planar exponential's asymptote. With R_g = r_face + g/2, k·g tends to n·N, so the engine's torque falls only about as 1/g while the physics falls as a steep power law. These rows are far outside the engine's gap sweep (corner gaps 0.5-4 mm; g/R_g up to about 3.3), and a 2% tolerance there says little about the engine's intended domain.

The 2% tolerance itself is a stated materiality policy, not an error in the check. So none of the members is a check_bug. They are two different model approximations:

- B: the empirical end factor has no real dependence on gap. Nothing else covers this. test_3d_end_effect_factor_across_lengths passes only because it runs at the default 1.4 mm gap, where f_end is off by just +0.4%.

Members 1, 2 (at 6-10 mm) and 3 should be regrouped under B.

verdicts.reason:
I reran all five members and they all fail as reported. They share one cause: the engine's free-space pull-out comes from the workbook's planar 2D slab model, and these checks compare it with a real curved, faceted 3D ring. The members are the gap sweep (-6.9% to +7.0%), the decay law, the pole sweep (+3.0% to -4.1%), the 2D long-length check (-3.9%) and the raw prototype (-3.8%).

The formula itself is implemented correctly. model.py geometry_factor, (1-e^-kt_i)(1-e^-kt_o)e^-kg/2, combined with tau_n = B_in·B_on/(2µ0)·S_n·sin(nπ/2), is the exact shear stress between two normally magnetized slab arrays with µr=1. I derived it independently from the surface-charge model and got the same result. The audit's own checks agree: test_planar_s_factor_is_exact_planar_limit and test_calculator_torque_chain_rederived both pass. What fails are the geometry comparisons: test_planar_s_factor_matches_cylindrical (curvature) and test_pullout_2d_matches_flat_block_reference (flat blocks on polygon faces versus a square-wave fill taken at R_g).

The pattern of errors fits an approximation, not a bug:
- The error changes sign across the gap and pole sweeps.
- It grows with gap/R_gap. The decay-law check diverges at face gaps of 30 and 100 mm because the planar e^-kg term, with k=n(N/2)/R_g and the 2πR_g² lever, cannot follow cylindrical and 3D multipole decay. Those gaps are far outside the design sweep's corner gaps of 0.5 to 4 mm.

The README declares all of this. "Approach" gives the exact planar formula with k = n·(poles/2)/R_gap, calls the model a "2D harmonic torque model", and says it "is an analytical estimate, not a guaranteed minimum". It also cites a much larger acknowledged 3D-versus-model gap (2.17 vs 2.85 N·m). model.py's docstring calls it "the workbook's 2D slab model". The engine also includes a one-point measured calibration for exactly this free-space prototype circuit, to absorb amplitude error. The README does not name curvature and facet shape specifically, so the wording could be sharper, but the approximation itself is documented.

This is not placeholder_input: none of the placeholder inputs is involved.

verdicts.proposed_correction:
No formula correction is needed; the engine matches the planar slab model it documents. There are two options:

1. Documentation only (recommended). Add a line to README "Approach" step 2 saying the shear stress uses the unrolled planar slab solution, which ignores ring curvature and flat-block (faceted) shape. In free space it differs from a 3D solution by roughly ±4-7% over the 0.5-4 mm corner-gap sweep, and it is not valid for gaps comparable to R_gap.

verdicts.reason:
I reproduced the finding from scratch, and the engine's own model contradicts it too, so it is a formula error and not just a 3D-versus-2D fidelity gap.

(1) Independent 3D check. I wrote my own magpylib model (scratch t3d.py) using the magnetic surface-charge method: the torque on the outer ring is (1/mu0) * sum over the outer blocks' radial faces of (J.n)(x*By - y*Bx) dA, with the field B taken from the inner ring only. Setup: 6 poles, default hub apothem 10.15 mm (the blocks fit), corner gap 1.0268 mm, B842SH 12.7 x 6.35 x 3.17 mm, Br 1.29 T, free space, 20 C. Result: peak |T| = 0.536784 N·m at 15.745 deg, and T at half a pitch (30 deg) = 0.328546 N·m. The ratio is 0.612, so evaluating at half a pitch gives -38.8% against the peak. With 16x16, 24x24 and 32x32 Gauss points the values agree to 3e-6 relative. This matches the audit's engine=0.3285457 and reference=0.5367842 to 7 digits.

(2) The engine's own harmonic model. model.shear_stress fixes the electrical angle at pi/2: tau_n = A_n * sin(n*pi/2), where A_n = B_in,n * B_on,n * S_n / (2*mu0). I maximised the engine's own curve T(x) = sum over n of A_n sin(n x) on a dense grid. Half a pitch is a local minimum whenever -A1 + 9*A3 - 25*A5 > 0, which is roughly A3/A1 > 1/9, as happens at low fill with few poles.
- 6 poles, apothem 10.15, free space: A3/A1 = 0.303. The model's own peak is at 15.88 deg mechanical (the 3D peak is at 15.74 deg), and the half-pitch value is 0.720 of the model's own maximum.
- Same case with back iron: A3/A1 = 0.165, and the half-pitch value is 0.945 of the maximum.
- 8 to 16 poles: half a pitch is the true maximum (A3/A1 between -0.04 and 0.02), which matches the audit's 0.000% rows.

So the pull-out is the value of the engine's own curve at a stationary point that is not its maximum. The single member has a single cause. The leftover difference after correction is T3-RC1: the corrected engine raw value of 0.470 is still -12.5% below the 3D peak, because the planar model's 3rd-harmonic amplitude is too small. That part is separate from this finding.

- Pull-out stays 2.6473 N·m, and the verdicts do not change.
- Default pole sweep: every row is unchanged. The 6-pole row, with its own hub of 9.2 mm, has A3/A1 = 0.094, so the correction ratio is 1.000. It stays 0.9584 N·m, "below hot minimum".
- The gap sweep is also unchanged.

Off-default cases where the correction matters:
- npole=6 with the default hub, back iron, 50 C: 0.8612 to 0.9109 N·m (+5.8%). The verdict stays "Below hot minimum".
- npole=6 with the default hub, free space, 20 C: raw 0.3385 to 0.4699 N·m (+38.8% as a factor, 1/0.720).

No verdict text changes in any case I checked.
verdicts.proposed_correction:
Take the pull-out as the maximum over angle of the model's own torque curve instead of its value at half a pitch.
- Let A_n = B_in,n * B_on,n * S_n / (2*mu0) for n = 1, 3, 5.
- Find x* = argmax over x in [0, pi] of sum over n of A_n sin(n x). Setting c = cos x, the condition dT/dx = 0 becomes A1*c + 3*A3*(4c^3 - 3c) + 5*A5*(16c^5 - 20c^3 + 5c) = 0. Its roots are c = 0 (half a pitch) plus the real roots of the remaining quartic in c. Evaluate T at every candidate and keep the largest. Dense sampling followed by a Newton step also works.
- Set tau_n = A_n * sin(n x*) and tau = sum of tau_n. Everything after that is unchanged: T = tau * 2*pi*R_g^2 * L * f_end * f_cal.
- Apply the same change to T_iron and T_noiron in model.compute and to sweeps._row, which also uses math.sin(n*pi/2).
- Optionally report the pull-out angle x*/(N/2).

Workbook cells: Calculator C76/C82/C88, and through them C89 and C91-C93, plus the pole and gap sweep columns.

verdicts.reason:
This group has one member, test_3d_peak_at_half_pole_pitch_across_pole_sweep. I looked for a bug in the check and found none; the failure is real.

The attack points I tested:
(1) Quadrature. With 1 mm/4-point panels the 3D torque at 6 poles is 0.328546 N·m at 30 deg and 0.536784 N·m at 15.74 deg. With 0.25 mm/6-point panels both values match to 1e-6.
(2) The single-block times N shortcut. Integrating all blocks (all_blocks=True) gives the same values.
(3) Peak finder. Dense scan points at 6, 9, 12, 15, 18 and 21 deg show a single maximum near 15.7 deg. A 41-point scan plus Brent refinement gives the same peak, 0.536784 N·m at 15.74 deg. The curve is exactly symmetric about 30 deg (T(27) = T(33), T(15.74) = T(44.26)), so 30 deg is a stationary point, but it is a local minimum, not the peak.
(4) Angle convention. The engine's npole is poles per ring, one block per pole, and k = n*(npole/2)/R_g. So sin(n pi/2) corresponds to half a pole pitch, which is 180/npole deg. The test's half_pitch = pi/npole matches.
(5) Geometry. The 6-pole case uses the default 10.15 mm hub. The engine accepts it: "OK, 5.37 mm slack" on the inner flats and blocks 10.65 mm apart at the outer faces. Fill is 0.517 inner and 0.372 outer. The 3D rings are built from the engine's own geometry fields.
(6) Engine field. The test labels 3D-at-half-pitch as "engine" on purpose, to separate the angle error from the amplitude error. That design is sound.

The strongest evidence is the engine's own harmonic model. Its torque-angle curve at this layout is T(x) = sum over n of A_n sin(n pi x / tau_p), with A1 = 38606, A3 = 11714 and A5 = -779 Pa. That curve peaks at x/tau_p = 0.265 (15.87 deg), almost the same angle as the 3D peak (15.74 deg). The engine's half-pitch value is only 0.720 of that peak. The cause is the large positive third harmonic at low fill, which is subtracted at half pitch because sin(3 pi/2) = -1.

So pull-out = torque at half a pitch disagrees with both the engine's own model and the 3D field. It is a fixed-angle evaluation error, not a check bug or a modelling limit. The 8-16 pole rows pass at 0.000%, which shows the harness is consistent. With back iron the same 6-pole/10.15 mm layout still has an engine-model peak shift (half/peak = 0.945). On the pole sweep's smallest-fitting hub (9.2 mm, free space) the 3D half/peak is 0.83, peaking at 41.8 deg.

None at the defaults (npole = 10, back iron). Half a pitch is the true maximum there, both in the engine model and in 3D (row error +0.000%). Pull-out stays 2.6473 N·m against a 2.5 N·m floor, and the verdict stays 'Nominal only: hot test'.

All six rows of the engine's default pole sweep (back iron, smallest-fitting hub 9.2-16.0 mm) also peak at half a pitch. Their values (0.958, 1.893, 2.568, 3.590, 4.766 and 6.096 N·m) and status strings are unchanged.

The calibration prototype (fill 0.884/0.631) also peaks at half a pitch, so f_cal is unaffected.

The error only matters for user layouts with low fill:
- 6 poles on the 10.15 mm hub in free space: the engine's own model understates its peak by 28%; against 3D the half-pitch torque is 39% below the peak.
- The same layout with back iron: about 5.5% low.
- 6 poles on the 9.2 mm hub in free space: about 5% low in the model and 17% low in 3D.
verdicts.proposed_correction:
Pull-out should be the maximum of the model's own torque-angle curve, not its value at half a pitch:

T_pull = AL * f_end * f_cal * max over x in (0, tau_p) of sum over n = 1, 3, 5 of [B_in * B_on * S_n / (2 mu0)] * sin(n pi x / tau_p)

This replaces the fixed sin(n pi/2) with sin(n pi x*/tau_p), where x* is the maximizer. It can be found by a 1-D bounded search, or by solving dT/dx = 0, which is a polynomial in cos(pi x / tau_p). When the third and fifth harmonics are small, x* = tau_p/2 and the result equals today's value.

Apply the change consistently in all places that use sin(n pi/2):
- model.shear_stress / Calculator C76, C82, C88 -> C93
- T_iron and T_noiron
- sweeps._row, columns N/Q/T -> X
- calibration.py tau_n

Nothing changes at the defaults. At 6 poles on the 10.15 mm hub in free space, the engine's raw pull-out rises by a factor of 1/0.7203 = 1.388, from 0.3385 to about 0.470 N·m. The 3D peak is 0.537 N·m, so the planar model's amplitude error (T3-RC1) remains.

verdicts.reason:
I reproduced all five members from scratch, and every member has the same cause: the engine's planar (flat-slab) harmonic model is being compared with real faceted cylindrical rings. The engine does not implement that model wrongly.

What I ran (scratch scripts in the session scratchpad: t3rc1.py, sweep.py, rest.py, cyl.py; no repo files touched):

(1) Engine side, derived independently. I worked out the free-space two-slab shear from the interaction energy. The field above slab 1 is B_y = (Br1n/2)(1-e^{-k t1}) e^{-k y} cos kx. Then W/area = -<M2.B1> integrated over slab 2, and tau_n = -dW/dd gives Br_in·Br_on/(4 mu0)·(1-e^{-k t_i})(1-e^{-k t_o})·e^{-k g}·sin(n k1 d). This is exactly the engine's S_free (with its /2) times Bi·Bo/(2 mu0). My own implementation, using R_g = r_face + g/2, fill at the mid-magnet radius and the 1-c_end·pitch/L end factor, reproduces the engine to every printed digit: T2D = 1.912786 and raw pull-out = 1.713773 N·m at defaults (free space, 20 C, 1.4 mm face gap).

(2) Correct value, computed a different way from the audit. I built magpylib Cuboid rings and took the torque as -dW/dtheta, where W = -∫ M·B_inner dV. That is my own composite Gauss-Legendre volume quadrature with a central difference. The audit instead integrates surface charges. I cross-checked against magpylib.getFT (1.777465 vs 1.777459) and refined the quadrature until values were stable to about 1e-7.

Results: every member reproduced exactly.
- Gap sweep, engine/3D - 1: -6.886%, -5.536%, -3.583%, -0.103%, +3.331%, +7.009%.
- Pole sweep for 6-16 poles: +3.044%, -4.088%, -3.583%, -2.342%, -1.238%, -0.393%.
- 2D limit (3D slope over L = 30-60 mm, times L): 1.991253 vs engine 1.912786, -3.941%.
- Prototype (hub 9.85 mm, 3D peak at exactly 18 deg): 1.755382 vs 1.688898, -3.787%.
- Decay ratios T(g)/T(1.4 mm) at 6, 10, 30 and 100 mm: +17.9%, +40.2%, +299%, +7101%.

(3) Where the error comes from. I also wrote the exact 2D cylindrical solution for radially magnetized arc rings with the same Br, fill and radii: T/L = pi·Bi·Bo·m²/(2 mu0 (m²-1))·(R2^{m+1}-R1^{m+1})(R3^{1-m}-R4^{1-m}). At 1.4 mm it gives 1.8874. The exact flat-block 2D value is 1.9913, and the planar model's 1.9128 sits between the two.
- At small gaps, faceting dominates. The inner block corners sit 0.37 mm closer than the face gap, so the engine reads low.
- At larger gaps, curvature dominates. Planar e^{-kg} decays more slowly than (R2/R3)^{m-1}, so the engine reads high. The sign flips near 2.4 mm.
- Harmonic truncation is negligible: 25 harmonics vs 3 changes the result by <0.1%.

The decay failure is out of the model's domain. At face gaps of 30-100 mm the outer ring would be 60-240 mm across, far outside the 43 mm envelope. There R_g grows with g, so k·g levels off near N and the planar torque tends to a small nonzero constant. The absolute engine value at 100 mm is 2.2e-4 N·m. Switching to the 'correct' cylindrical formula would not fix the design-gap error: it would be about -5.2% against the exact flat-block 2D value, worse than the engine's -3.9%. So no formula swap is clearly more accurate, and I found no engine_error.

- The Calibration measured correction: f_cal_updated = 1.0658 = measured/raw model. It is applied only to the no-iron, 10-pole, B842SH circuit, and there the one-point calibration absorbs the planar error. The raw error is -3.787% at the prototype and -3.583% at the design hub, so the calibrated free-space pull-out (1.8265 N·m at 20 C) carries only about a 0.2% residual bias from this cause.
verdicts.proposed_correction:
No engine formula change is warranted. Optional hardening for accuracy, not correctness:
(a) Document the planar model's known error band against 3D in free space: about -7% to +7% for corner gaps of 0.2-4 mm and pole counts of 6-16, and -3.9% for the 2D value at the defaults.
(b) Optionally flag or limit the model when g/R_gap is large (for example > 0.3). Beyond that the planar form levels off at a nonzero torque instead of vanishing.
(c) If better absolute accuracy is wanted, use a 3D- or 2D-exact-derived factor for the flat-block geometry. Replacing the slab formula with the arc-cylinder formula would not help: it moves the design-gap error from -3.9% to about -5.2%.

verdicts.reason:
I tried to break the checks and could not. The failures are real gaps between the model and the physics. The engine computes its documented formulas correctly, and the audit's reference is right.

(1) The 3D reference is sound. I rebuilt it by a separate method: the interaction energy -(J/mu0)*integral(B_r dV) over the outer block, differentiated in angle by finite difference. It matches torque_ref.ring_torque_3d to 7 significant figures at face gaps of 1.4, 4.4, 10 and 100 mm (for example 1.777459 N·m at 1.4 mm and 3.216426e-6 N·m at 100 mm). At 0.6 mm the two agree to 2e-5 using the fine quadrature the test uses. The 30-60 mm length-slope 2D reference is converged: moving it to 60-120 mm changes it by 4e-5 at 4.4 mm and 2e-4 at 10 mm.

(2) The geometry and angle match the engine. The rings are built from the engine's own C54/C56/C18-C30 fields. The block-centre radius a_i + t/2 is the same radius the engine uses for its fill factor. The comparison angle π/N is the engine's sin(nπ/2) pull-out point. The prototype check uses gap_definition=1 in both the engine and the audit.

(3) The engine's free-space S_n = (1-e^-kt_i)(1-e^-kt_o)e^-kg/2 with J_i·J_o/(2 mu0) matches my own derivation of two normally magnetized slabs under the surface-charge model. So this is not an engine error.

The members do not share one cause, though. I split each error into a 2D part and an end-factor part, using the 3D slope and T3D/(slope·L).
- Members 4 (-3.94%) and 5 (-3.79%, prototype) are purely the 2D harmonic amplitude. It is nearly constant at -3.8% to -4.2% for face gaps of 0.6-4.4 mm. This is the same cause as group 22 (test_pullout_2d_matches_flat_block_reference).
- Member 1 (gap sweep) gets its trend and its worst row from the end factor 1 - c_end·τp/L. That factor barely changes with gap, while the 3D end deficit grows with gap. At 4.4 mm the engine's f_end is 0.8848 against 0.7955 in 3D (+11.2%), on top of a 2D error of -3.8%, giving +7.0% overall. At 0.6 mm it is -3.2% on top of -3.8%, giving -6.9%.
- Member 3 (pole sweep): the worst row, 8 poles at -4.1%, is mostly end factor (f_end -3.4%, 2D -0.7%). At 6 poles a 2D error of +16.8% and an f_end error of -11.8% largely cancel.
- Member 2 (decay): the 6 mm and 10 mm rows come mostly from the end factor (+16.6% and +30.0%). The 30 mm and 100 mm rows come from the planar exponential's asymptote. With R_g = r_face + g/2, k·g tends to n·N, so the engine's torque falls only about as 1/g while the physics falls as a steep power law. These rows are far outside the engine's gap sweep (corner gaps 0.5-4 mm; g/R_g up to about 3.3), and a 2% tolerance there says little about the engine's intended domain.

The 2% tolerance itself is a stated materiality policy, not an error in the check. So none of the members is a check_bug. They are two different model approximations:
- A: the planar 2D amplitude is about 4% low.
- B: the empirical end factor has no real dependence on gap. Nothing else covers this. test_3d_end_effect_factor_across_lengths passes only because it runs at the default 1.4 mm gap, where f_end is off by just +0.4%.

Members 1, 2 (at 6-10 mm) and 3 should be regrouped under B.

verdicts.reason:
I reran all five members and they all fail as reported. They share one cause: the engine's free-space pull-out comes from the workbook's planar 2D slab model, and these checks compare it with a real curved, faceted 3D ring. The members are the gap sweep (-6.9% to +7.0%), the decay law, the pole sweep (+3.0% to -4.1%), the 2D long-length check (-3.9%) and the raw prototype (-3.8%).

The formula itself is implemented correctly. model.py geometry_factor, (1-e^-kt_i)(1-e^-kt_o)e^-kg/2, combined with tau_n = B_in·B_on/(2µ0)·S_n·sin(nπ/2), is the exact shear stress between two normally magnetized slab arrays with µr=1. I derived it independently from the surface-charge model and got the same result. The audit's own checks agree: test_planar_s_factor_is_exact_planar_limit and test_calculator_torque_chain_rederived both pass. What fails are the geometry comparisons: test_planar_s_factor_matches_cylindrical (curvature) and test_pullout_2d_matches_flat_block_reference (flat blocks on polygon faces versus a square-wave fill taken at R_g).

The pattern of errors fits an approximation, not a bug:
- The error changes sign across the gap and pole sweeps.
- It grows with gap/R_gap. The decay-law check diverges at face gaps of 30 and 100 mm because the planar e^-kg term, with k=n(N/2)/R_g and the 2πR_g² lever, cannot follow cylindrical and 3D multipole decay. Those gaps are far outside the design sweep's corner gaps of 0.5 to 4 mm.

The README declares all of this. "Approach" gives the exact planar formula with k = n·(poles/2)/R_gap, calls the model a "2D harmonic torque model", and says it "is an analytical estimate, not a guaranteed minimum". It also cites a much larger acknowledged 3D-versus-model gap (2.17 vs 2.85 N·m). model.py's docstring calls it "the workbook's 2D slab model". The engine also includes a one-point measured calibration for exactly this free-space prototype circuit, to absorb amplitude error. The README does not name curvature and facet shape specifically, so the wording could be sharper, but the approximation itself is documented.

This is not placeholder_input: none of the placeholder inputs is involved.

None on any headline number or verdict. The defaults use steel back iron (backiron=1), so pullout_Nm = 2.6473 N·m and the verdict "Nominal only: hot test" do not use the free-space S_n at all.

The free-space path at defaults only feeds two things:
- C96 pullout_noiron_Nm = 1.513 N·m, which is informational.
- The Calibration sheet. There the raw prototype model is 1.6889 N·m against 1.7554 N·m in 3D (-3.8%). That error is absorbed by f_cal_updated = 1.0658 (measured/model = 1.1219), and f_cal_updated is applied only to the no-iron prototype circuit. At that circuit the calibrated prediction is pinned to the 1.8 N·m measurement whatever the raw amplitude.

Within the design gap sweep the uncalibrated free-space amplitude error is between -6.9% and +7.0%. It is large only in the out-of-range decay test (30-100 mm).
verdicts.proposed_correction:
No formula correction is needed; the engine matches the planar slab model it documents. There are two options:

1. Documentation only (recommended). Add a line to README "Approach" step 2 saying the shear stress uses the unrolled planar slab solution, which ignores ring curvature and flat-block (faceted) shape. In free space it differs from a 3D solution by roughly ±4-7% over the 0.5-4 mm corner-gap sweep, and it is not valid for gaps comparable to R_gap.

2. Improve the model. Replace the planar S_n with the exact 2D cylindrical (r^±np) solution for arcs. That would remove the curvature part, but the facet-shape part would remain and it would break workbook parity, so it only makes sense if the workbook is updated too.

verdicts.reason:
I reproduced the finding. The engine is doing what its documented formula says, but the formula is being used where it no longer holds. The group has one member, test_3d_end_effect_factor_short_magnet.

What I ran:

(1) Engine at 20 °C, no back iron, manual magnets, L = 1 mm. The pole pitch is 2π·R_g/N with R_g = 14.02 mm and N = 10, which gives 8.8090 mm. The end factor is f_end = 1 − 0.15·8.8090/1.0 = −0.32135, and my hand calculation matches model.py:272 exactly. The resulting pull-out is −0.0460 N·m, which is physically impossible.

(2) An independent 3D reference, written from scratch in a temp script without the audit's torque_ref code:
- magpylib supplied only the analytic cuboid field of the inner ring.
- Torque on the outer ring comes from the interaction energy U = −(J/µ0)·Σ∫ n̂·B_inner dV, using a 3D Gauss-Legendre volume integral, with torque = −dU/dθ by central difference at half a pole pitch.
- This is a different method from the audit's surface-charge force integration.
- The 2D torque per length is the slope of T(L) between 30 and 60 mm (−156.79 N·m/m, converged to about 1e-4).
- The resulting 3D end factor f3D(L) = T(L)/(slope·L) is 0.2406 at L = 1 mm (0.24080 and 0.24064 at two quadrature levels). The audit reference is 0.24061, so the reference is correct.

The linear form f = 1 − c_end·τp/L against the 3D factor:

| L (mm) | Linear | 3D | Error |
|---|---|---|---|
| 12.7 | 0.8960 | 0.8926 | +0.4% |
| 3.17 | 0.5832 | 0.5785 | +0.8% |
| 2.0 | 0.339 | 0.428 | −21% |
| 1.5 | 0.119 | 0.342 | −65% |
| 1.0 | −0.321 | 0.241 | wrong sign |

So the root cause is not a coding slip. The workbook's empirical end factor is the first-order large-L form T = aL − b, and it gets steadily worse below about 3 mm (roughly 0.34·τp). It crosses zero at L = c_end·τp = 1.32 mm. The engine does not validate L, so it accepts inputs outside that range and returns a negative pull-out without any warning. That missing guard is a real defect worth fixing, but the numbers come from the approximation's domain, not from a wrong implementation.

Other places that use the same form, all at the default L = 12.7 mm:
- the gap and pole sweeps, W = 1 − c_end·I/L (sweeps.py:101);
- the calibration factor (calibration.py:86).

Their end factors are 0.838–0.908 and 0.898, all well inside the range where the form holds.

A 1 mm magnet with an 8.8 mm pole pitch is an extreme case the audit chose on purpose, not a placeholder input.
verdicts.impact_at_defaults:
None. The default active length is 12.7 mm. There, f_end = 0.8960 against 0.8926 in 3D (+0.4%), the pull-out is 2.647 N·m against a 2.5 N·m floor, and the verdict stays "Nominal only: hot test".

The default sweep and calibration end factors (0.838–0.908) are also in the range where the form holds.

Even in the L = 1 mm edge case, the verdict text does not change. The engine gives −0.046 N·m and "Below hot minimum". With the 3D factor the pull-out would be about 0.1506 × 0.2406 × 0.95 ≈ 0.034 N·m, which is still "Below hot minimum". Only the sign and size of the torque number are wrong.
verdicts.proposed_correction:
Keep the linear form (it is within 1% of 3D for L ≥ about 3 mm) and add a domain guard.

- Warn, or mark the status invalid, when L < about 0.34·τp (about 3 mm at defaults), which is where the linear form's error passes about 1%.
- Never allow f_end ≤ 0. Where L ≤ c_end·τp, raise an error or return NaN.
- Apply the guard to model.py:272, sweeps.py:101 and calibration.py:86.

If the engine has to return a value for every L > 0, one option is f = 1 − (ℓ/L)(1 − e^(−L/ℓ)), with ℓ = c_end·τp.
- It is positive for all L, tends to 1 − ℓ/L for large L, and to L/(2ℓ) for small L.

|---|---|---|

Correct value: I wrote my own script in the scratchpad (overhang3d.py). It builds the rings with magpylib Cuboids from the engine radii: inner centre 11.735 mm, outer centre 16.305 mm, t = 3.17 mm, w = 6.35 mm, 10 poles, Br = 1.29 T. It computes the torque with magpylib.getFT on meshed volumes. That is a different method from the audit's surface-charge quadrature. I computed it both ways: torque on the outer ring from the inner, and the reaction torque on the inner from the outer. At half a pole pitch, the equal-length torque is 1.7774 N·m and the 25.4 mm outer over 12.7 mm inner gives 2.0010 N·m. The ratio is 1.1258, converged to about 1e-4 over meshes of 1000 to 12000 cells. Physics: the 3D slope gives a 2D torque of 156.65 N·m per metre, or 1.9895 N·m at 12.7 mm. The equal-length 3D end factor is 0.893, which is close to the engine's 0.896. The 2D harmonic model with an empirical c_end end factor has no overhang term by construction. Ignoring overhang is a known, conservative simplification: the engine under-predicts. This is exactly the engine's S_free (with its /2) times Bi·Bo/(2 mu0). My own implementation, using R_g = r_face + g/2, fill at the mid-magnet radius and the 1-c_end·pitch/L end factor, reproduces the engine to every printed digit: T2D = 1.912786 and raw pull-out = 1.713773 N·m at defaults (free space, 20 C, 1.4 mm face gap).

I reran all five members and they all fail as reported. The members are the gap sweep (-6.9% to +7.0%), the decay law, the pole sweep (+3.0% to -4.1%), the 2D long-length check (-3.9%) and the raw prototype (-3.8%).

The formula itself is implemented correctly. model.py geometry_factor, (1-e^-kt_i)(1-e^-kt_o)e^-kg/2, combined with tau_n = B_in·B_on/(2µ0)·S_n·sin(nπ/2), is the exact shear stress between two normally magnetized slab arrays with µr=1. The pattern of errors fits an approximation, not a bug:
- The error changes sign across the gap and pole sweeps.
- It grows with gap/R_gap. The decay-law check diverges at face gaps of 30 and 100 mm because the planar e^-kg term, with k=n(N/2)/R_g and the 2πR_g² lever, cannot follow cylindrical and 3D multipole decay. Those gaps are far outside the design sweep's corner gaps of 0.5 to 4 mm.

The README declares all of this. "Approach" gives the exact planar formula with k = n·(poles/2)/R_gap, calls the model a "2D harmonic torque model", and says it "is an analytical estimate, not a guaranteed minimum". It also cites a much larger acknowledged 3D-versus-model gap (2.17 vs 2.85 N·m). model.py's docstring calls it "the workbook's 2D slab model". The engine also includes a one-point measured calibration for exactly this free-space prototype circuit, to absorb amplitude error. The README does not name curvature and facet shape specifically, so the wording could be sharper, but the approximation itself is documented.

This is not placeholder_input: none of the placeholder inputs is involved.

(1) The reference is sound. The 3D pull-out converges: with 0.25 mm panels, 6th-order quadrature and a 21-point angle scan, it moves by at most 3e-7 relative at the check's two gaps (1.767664 and 1.464880 N·m). The peak sits exactly at half a pitch. The reference also matches the bench: it gives 1.7554 N·m at the prototype's 1.4 mm flat gap, against 1.8 measured (-2.5%). I found no problem with units, fields, sign, Br (1.29 T at 20 °C) or geometry construction. prototype_geometry reproduces the engine's own C28-C33 values.

(2) The check reads the 1.0 and 1.5 mm gap labels on C47/C48 with the engine's "equivalent minimum corner gap" (a_o - r_corner, C30). That reading assumes the supplied 3D results are 16% above physics. Explaining that would need a stronger magnet (Br about 1.39 T, N48-class), not the stated B842SH (N42SH, 1.29-1.32 T). mu_r = 1.05 plus the top of the Br range gives at most about 5%.

(3) Read the same labels as flat face-to-face gaps instead. For parallel, equal-width blocks at alignment, that is also the corner-to-corner distance, a natural meaning of "corner gap" in an FEA model. Free-space 3D then gives 2.0419 N·m at 1.0 mm (supplied 2.06, -0.9%) and 1.6904 N·m at 1.5 mm (supplied 1.70, -0.6%). So the supplied torques themselves are fine, and the check's diagnosis ("supplied values 16% high") is misleading. The real defect is that the engine labels C47/C48 as minimum-corner-gap points and interpolates them in C49 at corner_gap (1.0185 mm at defaults) instead of at the flat gap (1.4 mm). The check inherits the engine's gap definition, so it is not a check bug in units, cells or numerics, though its framing needs rewording.

Confidence is moderate to high. This is an inference about how the external FEA defined its gap, but it rests on two independent points both matching within 1% under the flat reading, against a 16% unexplained offset under the corner reading.
